title: Cross-cloud conversational analytics made simple with open standards
raw_text:
The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting. Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards. BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue. In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language. Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration. The borderless lakehouse architecture This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms. When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access: Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define. Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform. All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service for Apache Spark . Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution. Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform. You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below. Configure Databricks Unity Catalog We begin in Databricks by preparing the catalog and table. In Unity Catalog, federated access requires that your target schema be associated with an external location registered in Databricks: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Databricks SQL workspace
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db;

-- Declare the managed target location at the schema level
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core 
 MANAGED LOCATION 's3://my-databricks-bucket/retail/data/';

-- Create the Iceberg dimension table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products (
 product_key INT,
 product_id STRING,
 product_name STRING,
 category STRING,
 subcategory STRING,
 brand STRING,
 price DOUBLE,
 cost DOUBLE
)
USING iceberg;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c564490>)])]> You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided in each section. Before external engines can read this table, a Databricks metastore administrator must enable External data access on the metastore details tab. Go to Databricks Admin account and under User Management, create a Databricks Service Principal and make a note of its UUID "6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" Connect Databricks to BigQuery Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Databricks workspace URL and the application ID of your Databricks service principal: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create dbx_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \
 --federated-catalog-type="unity" \
 --unity-instance-name="dbc-xxxxxxxx-xxxx.cloud.databricks.com" \
 --unity-catalog-name="dbx_retail_db" \
 --unity-service-principal-application-id="6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" \
 --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c80de90>)])]> Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned service account: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe dbx_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c80ddd0>)])]> Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Grant catalog traversal permission
GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG dbx_retail_db 
 TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;

-- Grant schema and read permissions
GRANT USE SCHEMA,EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA dbx_retail_db.dbx_core 
 TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987df65750>)])]> You must grant the EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA privilege to the Databricks Service Principal on the target schemas or catalog to enable credential vending for external data access. Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details - Issuer URL* - https://accounts.google.com Subject* - numeric subject ID returned by the catalog describe command eg 1124251400450xxxxxxxx Audiences - https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com Run one query across three clouds Federated Iceberg tables are addressed in BigQuery using four-part paths: project.catalog.namespace.table . In our environment, sales transactions reside natively in BigQuery: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS local_retail_dataset
OPTIONS(location="us-central1");

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` (
 sale_id STRING,
 sale_date DATE,
 customer_key INT64,
 product_key INT64,
 store_key INT64,
 quantity INT64,
 unit_price NUMERIC,
 discount NUMERIC,
 total_revenue NUMERIC,
 total_cost NUMERIC,
 margin NUMERIC
)
PARTITION BY sale_date
CLUSTER BY store_key, product_key;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c7dc650>)])]> We can now run a single SQL query joining our native sales transactions with customer records in Snowflake, product lines in Databricks, and store locations in AWS Glue: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT 
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name, -- From Snowflake Iceberg
 p.product_name, -- From Databricks Iceberg
 s.store_name, -- From AWS S3 Iceberg
 SUM(f.quantity) AS total_units_sold, -- From BigQuery native fact
 SUM(f.total_revenue) AS total_sales_revenue -- From BigQuery native fact
FROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c 
 ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p 
 ON f.product_key = p.product_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s 
 ON f.store_key = s.store_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY total_sales_revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c1377d0>)])]> BigQuery processes the joins in place. Notice that Snowflake identifiers appear in uppercase ( CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS ), while Databricks and AWS Glue maintain lowercase table paths. Figure 2 - Query results combining data across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue. Explore cross-cloud data with natural language Because federated Iceberg tables behave like native tables within BigQuery, downstream analytical features inherit access directly. You can point conversational analytics in BigQuery at these federated schemas to let team members explore cross-cloud data using natural language prompts. To give conversational analytics full operational context, we save our federated join as a logical view: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.v_omnichannel_sales_pulse` AS
SELECT 
 f.sale_id,
 f.sale_date,
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name,
 c.country AS customer_country,
 p.product_name,
 p.category AS product_category,
 p.brand AS product_brand,
 s.store_name,
 s.city AS store_city,
 s.region AS store_region,
 f.quantity,
 f.total_revenue,
 f.margin
FROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c 
 ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p 
 ON f.product_key = p.product_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s 
 ON f.store_key = s.store_key;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c136e90>)])]> Analyze sales performance in natural language When you ask conversational analytics in BigQuery: "Who are our top customers by total sales revenue, what products did they buy, and which stores did they shop at?" Conversational analytics evaluates the schema across all three remote catalogs, generates the SQL statement, executes the query, and presents the response. Figure 3: Conversational analytics in BigQuery translates plain-language prompts into federated queries across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue. Plan for caching and data residency Before deploying federated catalogs in production, consider these operational behaviors: Background refresh timing: The --refresh-interval flag controls metadata synchronization. The minimum interval is 300 seconds. For larger catalogs containing hundreds of tables, metadata retrieval can take longer. If a sync cycle overruns, BigQuery skips the next scheduled run to avoid task queuing. Automatic query caching: BigQuery caches retrieved cross-cloud data blocks in the region where your federated catalog resides (e.g. us-central1 ). This helps reduce network transfer on repeated queries. Because cached blocks reside within Google Cloud storage in that region, confirm that this aligns with your organization's data residency policies. Encryption controls: Cross-cloud cache blocks use Google-managed encryption keys. If your organization enforces the constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices policy constraint, BigQuery bypasses the cache and reads directly from remote storage for every query. Monitoring access metrics: You can evaluate cache utilization in your query execution plans. Check the objectStorageStats section in BigQuery job statistics to compare cacheBytesRead against objectStorageBytesRead . Next steps In summary, Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse helps you activate your data regardless of where it lives without costly migrations or building additional data pipelines. Get started today by reviewing the borderless Lakehouse architecture documentation to learn more about supported regions and credential configurations. You can work through the borderless Lakehouse codelab to practice federating external catalogs step-by-step. Finally, connect with your Google Cloud account team or customer engineer to evaluate borderless lakehouse patterns for your specific data platforms or industries. Appendix Setting up Snowflake and AWS Glue cross cloud data access Connect Snowflake and Big Query Configure Snowflake Horizon Catalog We begin in Snowflake by creating the database, schema, and Iceberg table. In Snowflake Horizon, managed Iceberg tables expose an open Apache Iceberg REST catalog interface automatically: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db.core;

-- Create the Iceberg dimension table
CREATE OR REPLACE ICEBERG TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers (
 customer_key INTEGER,
 customer_id VARCHAR,
 first_name VARCHAR,
 last_name VARCHAR,
 email VARCHAR,
 gender VARCHAR,
 country VARCHAR,
 signup_date DATE

)
CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE'
EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c137f10>)])]> Before external engines can read this catalog, configure a dedicated reader role and grant traversal permissions across the database, schema, and table. SQL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Create a dedicated reader role
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;

-- Grant database and schema traversal permissions
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sf_retail_db TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sf_retail_db.core TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;

-- Grant read access on the target table
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c137b50>)])]> Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Snowflake account identifier, the reader role, and the root Iceberg database name: bash code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create sf_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \
 --federated-catalog-type="snowflake" \
 --snowflake-account-identifier="xy12345-ab67890" \
 --snowflake-warehouse="SF_RETAIL_DB" \
 --snowflake-role="gcp_lakehouse_reader_role" \
 --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c135150>)])]> In the Apache Iceberg REST specification, --snowflake-warehouse references the catalog root database name ( SF_RETAIL_DB ), not a virtual compute warehouse. Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned numeric service account ID: bash code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe sf_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --format='value(biglake-service-account-id)''), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c136990>)])]> Return to Snowflake to bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user via Workload Identity Federation (WIF): SQL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

-- Bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user
CREATE OR REPLACE USER snowflake_service_user
 TYPE = SERVICE
 WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = (
 TYPE = GCP
 SUBJECT = '102669xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx' -- Numeric subject ID returned by gcloud describe
 )
 DEFAULT_ROLE = gcp_lakehouse_reader_role
 COMMENT = 'Service user for Lakehouse catalog federation over WIF';

-- Grant the reader role to this service user
GRANT ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role TO USER snowflake_service_user;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987c9a3fd0>)])]> This establishes passwordless authentication over OpenID Connect, allowing BigQuery to discover table metadata and vend temporary query-time credentials directly from Snowflake Horizon. Configure AWS Glue Data Catalog We begin in AWS by preparing the IAM identity, establishing access permissions across AWS Glue and Amazon S3, and registering the Iceberg table. First, create a placeholder trust policy named trust_policy.json . This allows you to provision the AWS IAM role before Google Cloud assigns the unique catalog service agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '{

 "Statement": [
 {

summary: The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting. Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse.

title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems

title: Agentic data science with the Data Agent Kit
raw_text:
Imagine your compliance team notices that payments are taking longer than expected to clear. They suspect fraud, and you’re the data scientist helping figure out which transactions to investigate first. Assembling that shortlist requires ingesting and cleaning raw transaction logs, training a model on past fraud, scoring new records, and scheduling the pipeline to run daily. Here’s how you can build that workflow end to end with an agent, using the Data Agent Kit inside the Antigravity IDE. Introducing the Data Agent Kit Data Agent Kit helps you work with Google Cloud data through a plugin for coding agents or an extension for Visual Studio Code-based IDEs . It brings two significant additions to the workflow: Help for your agent: MCP tools connect your agent to data services. Skills are Markdown files that give it instructions and best practices for working with your data stack Tools in your IDE: work with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud , from querying databases to deploying an Airflow pipeline, without leaving your editor Loading the data Let’s start with the raw transaction logs in Google Cloud Storage . You can ask the agent to create a notebook that loads them into BigQuery using Spark : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to ingest JSON transaction logs from gs://financials-clearing-raw/ into the BigQuery table transactions.raw_transactions.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987eb2d5d0>)])]> The agent generates a Jupyter notebook that loads the JSON logs into a BigQuery table named raw_transactions . You can open the notebook, review the code, and run it using a preconfigured Spark Serverless runtime from the IDE. Running a generated PySpark notebook After the notebook runs, you can open the raw_transactions table with the Data Agent Kit. The extension allows you to browse the table and inspect its metadata right from the IDE. Inspecting a BigQuery table in the IDE The records are now in BigQuery, but they aren’t ready for model training yet. First, we’ll handle duplicate and incomplete records, then join the remaining records with info about who sent and received each payment. Cleaning it up Let’s put the cleanup logic into a dbt project so we can run it on each new batch of data. We’ll also test that each transaction appears only once. Prompt the agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a dbt project in dbt_project/ for the BigQuery dataset transactions.

Deduplicate raw_transactions by transaction_id in staging. Separate records with null IDs into invalid_transactions. Join valid records with dim_payers and dim_payees to create enriched_transactions, preserving the is_fraud label. Add a transaction uniqueness test.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987eb2f910>)])]> The agent generates a dbt project with SQL models for cleaning and enriching the data. Take a look at the generated code to check how it handles duplicates and joins reference tables. Then run dbt build in the terminal. This builds the staging and enriched tables in BigQuery, along with a separate table for records with missing transaction IDs. dbt also runs the uniqueness test. Validating dbt models in the integrated terminal We also keep the is_fraud column, which indicates whether a past transaction was fraudulent. We’ll train the model on records with known labels and use it to score new transactions, where we’re unsure yet whether fraud occurred. Building the review queue With the data prepared, let’s ask the agent to create a training notebook using a Random Forest classifier running on Spark Serverless. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to train a RandomForestClassifier
on table transactions.enriched_transactions.

Predict is_fraud, training only on records where the label
is not null. Encode categorical features, scale amounts,
and evaluate the model using ROC AUC. Save the evaluated model to gs://models/fraud_model.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987eb2c950>)])]> Review and run the notebook, then check its evaluation output to see how well the model separates fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones. You can also use the Data Agent Kit extension to verify that the trained model artifacts were saved to Google Cloud Storage. Verifying the trained model artifacts in Google Cloud Storage Now we can use the saved model to score transactions that don’t have an is_fraud value yet: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a batch inference notebook that loads the saved model from gs://my_models/fraud_model and scores records in transactions.enriched_transactions where is_fraud is null.

Write transactions with a fraud probability score >= 0.50 to the Spanner table SparkEvalFraudReviewQueue, in the instance cymbal-fraud, database fraud-db.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987eb2f810>)])]> In this example, the inference notebook scores the unlabeled transactions in BigQuery and sends those with an estimated fraud probability of 50% or higher to the Spanner review queue. The flagged records help the team decide where to investigate, but they still need to determine whether fraud occurred. Look at how the inference notebook filters and writes flagged records, then run it. Once it finishes, query the Spanner table in the IDE to inspect the results. Querying flagged transactions in the Spanner table This table is the list we set out to build. The compliance team can now start reviewing transactions, and we have a workflow that gets records from raw logs into the queue. So far, we have been kicking off each step ourselves. We can now connect them so the workflow runs automatically each day. Running it again tomorrow Each day we will load the latest logs, apply the dbt transformations, and score unlabeled transactions using the saved model. We’ll use the Managed Service for Apache Airflow to run these steps in order. Ask the agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create an orchestration pipeline named fraud_analysis_pipeline that runs ingestion, the dbt project, and batch inference in that order.

Schedule it daily at midnight. Use Spark Serverless for the notebooks, including the Spanner connector for inference, and gs://YOUR_ARTIFACT_BUCKET for artifact storage.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987eb2de90>)])]> The agent generates a YAML pipeline definition and deployment configuration. The pipeline definition sets the schedule and dependencies between steps. Meanwhile, the deployment configuration specifies the Airflow environment where it will run. Data Agent Kit then turns the definition into an Airflow DAG, which you can explore as an interactive graph in the IDE. Open the pipeline under “Orchestration Pipelines” and click a task to inspect it. For notebook tasks, you can follow the link straight back to the code. Inspecting a data pipeline With the Airflow environment configured, click “Run pipeline” in the canvas. Data Agent Kit packages the notebooks and dbt project, deploys the DAG, and triggers a run. Open the pipeline’s execution history to follow its progress. You can also select individual tasks to inspect their status, duration, and logs. Kicking off an Airflow DAG and inspecting the logs Airflow will run the pipeline every day, taking new batches of data from raw logs to the review queue. The compliance team can now focus on flagged transactions, and you’ve automated the work of getting those records to them! Try it yourself If you are ready to try this for yourself, we have designed a codelab that walks you through the full setup so you can build and run this workflow. You can also read our documentation or check out the skills and tools in the open-source repository on GitHub . title: 10 Years of the SRE book: Announcing the second edition of "Site Reliability Engineering”
raw_text: A decade ago, Google released Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems with O'Reilly Media. What began as a collection of our practices for managing large-scale infrastructure became a bestselling book, and inspired many organizations to adopt the reliability practices it outlined: applying software engineering to operations to build systems that are scalable, reliable, and sustainable. Over the past ten years, computing landscapes have undergone profound shifts. AI, microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless paradigms, and platform engineering have all reshaped how we build and operate software. To mark the 10th anniversary of the book's release, we are excited to announce the completely rewritten second edition of the Google SRE book, reflecting a decade of lessons learned both inside Google and across the broader industry, to offer fresh guidance tailored for today's operational challenges. Why update the book? When we published the first edition, many organizations were focused on early cloud migrations and just starting to transition from monolithic architectures. Today, with organizations delivering software at a high velocity and at global scale, the challenge is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining high reliability in the face of the immense complexity. Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before. The explosion of resource-intensive workloads like generative AI has changed the economics and operational requirements of infrastructure management. Writing this second edition required us to take a step back and evaluate what it takes to successfully implement SRE today. A decade of evolution: How SRE practices have progressed The second edition takes a deep dive into how foundational site reliability engineering practices have matured over the last ten years, shifting from manual, task-specific work toward automated, platform-wide capabilities. Consider, for example: SLOs and error budgets: In 2016, teams relied on basic availability metrics and manual error budget policies. Today, practices have matured into user-centric, multi-tiered SLOs with dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Monitoring and observability: Early setups centered on static dashboards, basic logs, and manual alert triage. Modern observability leverages OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing, and automated anomaly correlation to find root causes quickly. Automation and platforms: Operations have shifted from writing custom scripts for isolated tasks to using declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms, and resilient, self-healing systems. Reliability testing: Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification. Capacity and resource management: Manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment, and dedicated cost and cluster optimization for GPU and TPU workloads. Organizational models: SRE has expanded beyond dedicated teams assigned to specific applications. Today's organizations use hybrid models, platform engineering integrations, and reliability champions embedded across product teams. SRE in the age of AI Then there’s the dual relationship between SRE and artificial Intelligence: how SRE supports AI infrastructure, and how SRE teams use AI to enhance operational reliability. Running large language models (LLMs) and foundation models introduces novel reliability challenges. The book outlines methodologies for operating AI infrastructure at scale: Managing massive GPU and TPU hardware cluster reliability and network topologies Monitoring non-deterministic outputs and latency characteristics unique to AI Ensuring pipeline reliability for continuous model training, fine-tuning, and data processing AI is also rapidly becoming a force multiplier for reliability engineers. The second edition shares practical frameworks for enhancing human operational efficiency: Using generative AI tools to assist in real-time incident triage and postmortem generation Interrogating complex system telemetry using natural language queries Using predictive machine learning models to identify resource bottlenecks before outages occur What hasn’t changed? The importance of culture While technologies and architectures continuously evolve, the core principles of SRE remain intact, and are key to establishing a reliability-focused culture. Accordingly, the second edition re-emphasizes and expands upon the human elements of system engineering, and how to get there. Whether you’re new to the field, a practitioner, an engineering manager, or a technology executive, the rewritten second edition of Site Reliability Engineering serves as your definitive roadmap for the next era of production systems. You can order your copy today in physical format (see Google Books ) or digital format from O'Reilly .

Either way, the solution has always been to build a custom application. The advent of AI has sped up the process — a working prototype now takes an afternoon — but the excitement of that first demo fades fast. Without access to governed data, row-level security, an infrastructure owner, or a clear path through security review, a tool written by an LLM is simply a prototype that can never go to production. Today, to bridge this gap, we are announcing Looker Data Apps (in preview) — pairing the speed of agent-generated applications with the governance, security, and trust of your existing Looker governance framework. Describe what you need in plain language, and the agent builds it as a real, production-grade application hosted natively inside Looker! What is a data app? A data app is a bespoke, interactive web application generated by an AI agent and hosted natively within Looker. While dashboards provide top-down visibility, data apps serve as an active system of action designed around a specific operational workflow. A data app: Goes beyond standard grid tiles with pixel-perfect, bespoke layouts configured for a specific operational role or job-to-be-done. Enables business users to input parameters, test scenarios, run live simulations, and update underlying records. Connects end-to-end business processes by connecting data analysis to business execution tasks like updating source records or dispatching events to tools like Salesforce and Jira. Build pixel-perfect interfaces using AI developer tools like Claude Code or Antigravity CLI, grounded directly by Looker’s semantic layer. Expanding your semantic layer into an application platform Data apps do not replace dashboards; they expand the boundaries of what you can build on top of your existing dashboards and semantic layer. Dashboards excel at aggregate visibility and passive reporting. Data apps handle active execution, letting users modify parameters and trigger downstream business tasks. Dashboards provide consistency using standardized chart libraries. Data apps deliver broad flexibility, unlocking custom web components and specialized interactions. Data apps are grounded in governed data to ensure accuracy. Whether users are reviewing a KPI dashboard or adjusting budgets in a data app, all logic is governed centrally with the LookML semantic layer to eliminate metric discrepancies and hallucinations. Transform analysis into action with customizable, multi-page web app experiences and embedded operational workflows. title: Introducing TimesFM 3.0 with multivariate time-series forecasting in BigQuery
raw_text:
Overview Since introducing zero-shot time-series forecasting in BigQuery with AI.FORECAST — initially powered by TimesFM 2.0 and later upgraded to TimesFM 2.5 — you have been able to generate forecasts directly in SQL without training or managing custom models. However, up until TimesFM 2.5, these foundation models were limited to univariate forecasting, predicting future values from the history of a single time series alone. In practice, most real-world forecasting problems are multivariate, where related targets and external drivers like weather, promotions, and holidays jointly shape future outcomes. Today, we are thrilled to announce the preview of TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery. Developed by Google Research, TimesFM 3.0 is a 330-million parameter state-of-the-art foundation model designed to unlock native multivariate time-series forecasting directly inside BigQuery SQL. TimesFM 3.0 ranks #1 across all three major public time-series leaderboards — GIFT-Eval, FEV-Bench, and TIME — achieving top zero-shot accuracy on both covariate and multivariate forecasting tasks compared to existing foundation models. Alongside its new multivariate capabilities, TimesFM 3.0 also serves as a drop-in upgrade for univariate forecasting via AI.FORECAST and anomaly detection via AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES . Existing workflows can immediately benefit from higher benchmark accuracy simply by specifying model => 'TimesFM 3.0' . What’s new: Multivariate foundation modeling With TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings enterprise-grade multivariate modeling into familiar SQL workflows via AI.FORECAST: Capability TimesFM 2.0 / 2.5 TimesFM 3.0 Forecasting scope Univariate only Univariate and multivariate Target columns Single target Single or multiple targets Covariate columns with past-only values Not supported Supported Covariate columns with past and future values Not supported Supported Multivariate forecasting with BigQuery SQL To see how these capabilities work together, let’s forecast daily commuter (subscriber_trips) and leisure (casual_trips) bike rides over a seven-day horizon using the NYC Citi Bike public dataset ( bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips ). BigQuery uses a single-table input format for multivariate forecasting that combines two sets of rows: Historical observation rows : timestamps between start time (2016-01-01) and the forecast cutoff date (2016-06-01), fully populated with target metrics, past covariates, and known future covariates Future horizon rows : timestamps across the seven-day forecast horizon (2016-06-01 to 2016-06-07) populated with known future covariates, while target columns and past-only covariates are set to NULL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "WITH data AS (
 SELECT
 DATE(starttime) AS date,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Subscriber'), NULL) AS subscriber_trips,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Customer'), NULL) AS casual_trips,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', AVG(tripduration / 60.0), NULL) AS avg_duration_min,
 IF(EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM MIN(starttime)) IN (1, 7), 1.0, 0.0) AS is_weekend
 FROM `bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips`
 WHERE starttime >= '2016-01-01' AND starttime < '2016-06-08'
 GROUP BY date
)
SELECT
 *
FROM
 AI.FORECAST(
 TABLE data,
 MODEL => 'TimesFM 3.0',
 TIMESTAMP_COL => 'date',
 TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'],
 PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'],
 FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend']
 );"), ('language', 'lang-sql'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f987caa06d0>)])]> This query highlights the three multivariate dimensions supported in TimesFM 3.0: Forecasting correlated targets ( target_cols ) Instead of running separate models for each rider segment, passing TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'] forecasts both metrics jointly in a single call. TimesFM 3.0 captures the cross-series dynamics between commuter and casual riders — such as shared weather sensitivity and diverging weekend ridership patterns. Using past covariates ( past_covariate_cols ) Some signals can only be observed historically and are not known in advance, such as average ride duration (avg_duration_min), historical foot traffic, or unplanned service disruptions. Passing PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'] (with future horizon rows set to NULL) gives the model historical context to distinguish temporary shocks from underlying trends without requiring future values for that feature. Using future covariates ( future_covariate_cols ) Other external drivers are known ahead of time across both the historical window and the forecast horizon — such as weekends (is_weekend), holidays, or scheduled promotions. Passing FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend'] (populated across all rows through 2016-06-07) allows TimesFM 3.0 to condition its seven-day predictions directly on upcoming calendar events. Understanding the output The function returns structured predictions for each target column specified in target_cols . For each column in target_cols, AI.FORECAST returns a struct containing the point forecast (value) and the lower and upper prediction interval bounds: date subscriber_ trips.value subscriber_trips.prediction_ interval_lower_bound subscriber_trips.prediction_ interval_upper_bound casual_trips.value casual_trips.prediction_ interval_lower_bound casual_trips.prediction_ interval_upper_bound time_series_type confidence_level ai_forecast_status 2016-06-01 00:00:00 UTC 44699.64 32590.76 55723.44 4581.32 1727.91 9189.31 forecast 0.95 2016-06-02 00:00:00 UTC 44611.75 30413.05 57209.19 4647.17 1466.23 10273.55 forecast 0.95 2016-06-03 00:00:00 UTC 41379.15 26218.65 54940.09 5341.36 1568.23 11805.86 forecast 0.95 2016-06-04 00:00:00 UTC 30164.34 14266.43 45075.92 9097.74 2558.27 18452.52 forecast 0.95 2016-06-05 00:00:00 UTC 26727.27 10101.44 42239.33 8398.50 1692.15 17768.99 forecast 0.95 2016-06-06 00:00:00 UTC 36713.84 19493.00 52679.59 4723.08 400.08 11710.73 forecast 0.95 2016-06-07 00:00:00 UTC 39749.97 22157.42 56119.86 4180.97 95.70 10845.74 forecast 0.95 TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics You can also run multivariate forecasts using natural language in BigQuery Conversational Analytics. On the same bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips dataset, you can simply ask "Forecast both daily subscriber and casual trips for June 1–7, 2016 using two month historical data, with average trip duration as a past covariate and weekend indicator as a future covariate." Conversational Analytics automatically generates and executes the underlying AI.FORECAST query with TimesFM 3.0, returning a summary of the results, interactive forecast charts with prediction intervals for each target, and key forecast insights. title: OpenAI’s AI misalignment problem is growing
raw_text: OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse , based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors. In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets. These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces. The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI. In his personal blog , for instance, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the industry must “step back and assess the trust architecture for this new era.” Destroying its own testing environment OpenAI began more aggressive misalignment monitoring following the July 2026 Hugging Face incident , in which autonomous OpenAI research agents broke out of their sandboxes and targeted Hugging Face infrastructure. Hundreds of its agents also attacked the RubyGems platform and targeted German programming wiki sites in recent months. In one of its new reports, OpenAI describes how an internal model, tasked with grading several other models, figured out how to damage its own environment when it couldn’t arrive at intended results. When comparing seven responses from seven different models, the grader had to inspect the conversational context and work behind each response, and to include information pointing back to input files. The model was instructed: Conversation context is **required** grading input, not optional background. It discovered that required input files were missing, nevertheless, it tried to submit assessments with no supporting information. These were rejected by an automated check. The model also created seven fake conversation files and seven fake response files containing fabricated information; these were rejected, too. “It considered submitting arbitrary scores, despite recognizing that it lacked the evidence to grade and that ‘random scoring’ was ‘unethical,’” OpenAI explained. The model also tested the automated check by submitting placeholder reports to learn what information a report had to contain and how many responses it was expected to grade. After these failures, the model decided to damage its task environment, presumably with the hope that the host would replace it with one containing the missing inputs. It deleted software required to run its tools and tried to remove system directories. Although automated checks rejected its incorrect or made-up grades, “this incident illustrates why monitoring must also cover the grader’s actions, including attempts that fail or crash without producing an accepted result,” OpenAI wrote. Breaking the rules to get the right answers, hiding the evidence In another instance, an OpenAI model developed and tested ways to bypass internet access restrictions. The model was asked questions about teacher salaries, electrical grid connections, and disability counts in specific areas. It was limited to using basic HTTP GET data retrieval requests, but “the model sometimes treated this restriction as something to circumvent,” OpenAI explained. It explored other ways to contact outside resources, for instance, determining whether its proxy intermediary service could carry other kinds of connections, or if outside services could make requests on its behalf. In some cases, it continued to probe these other options even when it had the statistics it needed. “These cases show that a model may continue developing ways around access restrictions even when additional access is unnecessary to obtain the information it needs,” OpenAI wrote. In a third instance, also involving public statistics, OpenAI models figured out how to bypass restrictions on internet access and get access to numbers from public government data sources. The models in this experiment were also restricted to HTTP GET requests, but they “wrote custom programs to send other types of requests,” OpenAI explained. Using one of these programs, a model queried a publicly-available dashboard, and even as it “explicitly recognized” that its actions violated its restrictions, it continued collecting much more data than it required. Later, it decided not to disclose what it had done. Another model used a temporary email address to create and verify an account for a site, then downloaded publicly available data. “These cases illustrate why correct answers are not enough to establish that a model behaved appropriately,” OpenAI wrote. “A model may obtain accurate information through prohibited methods, and deliberately conceal how it did so.” In response to these incidents, and others, OpenAI says it has hardened security controls, taken “additional steps” to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, and improved alignment grading. It has also “extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic.”

title: IonQ’s $1.2 billion acquisition of Elisity is trying to position it for quantum cybersecurity
raw_text: When quantum vendor IonQ on Sunday announced a $1.2 billion all stock deal to take over cybersecurity vendor Elisity, it spoke of a near-term future where enterprise quantum cybersecurity needs will move beyond replacing to-be-outdated encryption. The acquisition brings together IonQ’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities and Elisity’s enterprise Zero Trust technology platform, IonQ said in a news release . “On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.” The news release pointed to more than 100 global Elisity customers, and said IonQ expects to receive “expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation market.” Analysts and consultants saw the move as having potential, but pointed to technical challenges of truly integrating the product lines. “What IonQ gets today is access. Dividing the headline price by those deployments puts it at about $13 million each,” said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “That is a steep price for a Rolodex, if you will. Paying in its own stock makes the price easier for IonQ to swallow.” Dickson said that Elisity, which was founded in 2019, has focused on zero trust microsegmentation. “In plain terms, it limits each user, device, workload, and AI agent to only the network connections it needs. An attacker who gets in cannot roam freely,” Dickson said. “Its software enforces those rules over the network a customer already owns, without new hardware. That is a solid business aimed at attacks happening today. Little of it has anything to do with quantum.” Justin Greis , CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that the pairing could be effective for enterprise CISOs, assuming the internal tech integration issues can be overcome. “Bringing those capabilities together could create a compelling platform, particularly as enterprises contend with increasingly complex environments, autonomous AI agents, and a growing number of non-human identities,” Greis said. “But these are different layers of protection, and integrating them into a cohesive offering will require meaningful engineering and execution.” Brian Jackson , a principal research director at Info-Tech Research Group, also noted that part of the move speaks to IonQ’s need for revenue while quantum is ramping up. “IonQ’s core quantum computing business is still years from broad commercial payoff, so this reads as a move to build revenue in adjacent security markets where customers are already buying,” he said. “The quantum link is thinner than the announcement suggests. Post-quantum cryptography runs on classical systems, so migration depends on cryptographic inventory and crypto-agility, not quantum computing expertise.” Paul Smith-Goodson , VP/principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, agreed that the potential benefits from the acquisition are real, but he added that quantum requirements from the US government are also a key factor. “At the architectural level, integrating Elisity with IonQ’s PQC and QKD establishes an end-to-end defense capable of neutralizing future CRQC [Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer] threats,” Smith-Goodson said. “Elisity also hands IonQ an immediate, established enterprise sales pipeline of trusted CISO relationships. That will allow IonQ to cross-sell its broader quantum portfolio and capitalize on federal PQC migration mandates.”

title: October Patch Tuesday roundup: Over 1,400 Microsoft holes to be plugged, including three zero days
raw_text: Microsoft released a record-shattering 1,407 CVEs to be plugged today on October Patch Tuesday, breaking the 2020 record of 1,261. The list was so long that its release was several hours later than the usual 1 p.m. Eastern drop time, somewhat frustrating admins. The bugs include three zero-day vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited. The zero day being exploited, and that should be dealt with immediately, is CVE-2026-96951 , a security flaw that bypasses the Mark of the Web (MotW) protections in Windows Shell. This is the third flaw in Windows Shell that has been exploited in the wild this year, noted Satnam Narang , senior staff research engineer at Tenable. The others are CVE-2026-21510 , which is linked to the advanced persistent threat group APT28 (also known as Fancy Bear ), and CVE-2026-32202 , a known exploited vulnerability which was a fix for an incomplete patch for CVE-2026-21510 . “There have been 26 Windows Shell vulnerabilities patched in 2026 through October,” said Narang, “a staggering figure compared to previous years, with only three Windows Shell CVEs in 2025, and just one in 2024 and 2022.” Another zero day is a hole in SharePoint ( CVE-2026-102866 ) which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. The third zero day is CVE-2026-108398 , an untrusted search path in Windows’ .Net framework that allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control enforcement. This could lead to the ability to run unauthorized applications on target systems. Among other vital patches, developers running self-managed instances of GitLab should quickly patch their servers to plug a hole that could allow an unauthenticated user to exploit arbitrary code through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. GitLab has remediated this issue in its hosted instance. “ CVE-2026-97229 puts a critical part of the software supply chain at risk,” commented Gene Moody , Field CTO at Action1. Treat this hole as an emergency, he said, and immediate patch self-managed instances . Critical IBM bugs IBM is warning that a critical vulnerability has been found in its IBM i versions 7.3, 7.4, 7.5 and 7.6 operating systems for Power Systems hardware. The hole, CVE-2026-96119 with a CVSS score of 9.9, allows a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code due to improper data sanitization in the HTTP Server Administration Graphical User Interface (GUI). IBM strongly recommends that the vulnerability be patched immediately. Users of unsupported versions of the OS should upgrade to supported and fixed versions. Attacks on Atlassian self-hosted products Atlassian reported exploitation attempts that also warrant immediate patching and log review, said researchers at Nightwing. CVE-2026-21589 affects eight self-hosted products, including Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket. An unauthenticated attacker who knows an exact filename and path can read specific files inside the application’s web root; sensitive configuration files could expose information useful for further intrusion. There are reports that exploitation attempts began October 6, although attempts do not establish successful customer compromise. Patch every affected installation, Nightwing advised, including applicable cluster nodes and mirrors. If patching is delayed, restrict external access and apply Atlassian’s temporary mitigation; a normal login does not block this flaw. Review access logs and rotate secrets where exposure is suspected. Atlassian Cloud is patched, and requires no user action. Microsoft patches Researchers at Nightwing drew attention to four updates for on-premises Exchange Server, each of which fixes a high severity vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. “While each update addresses only a single CVE, the 8.8 CVSS score signals a serious risk, likely involving privilege escalation or remote exploitation potential,” Nicholas Carroll , Nightwing’s cyber incident response manager said. “Exchange admins should prioritize testing and deployment of these patches, given the historical track record of Exchange vulnerabilities being actively targeted in the wild.” Nightwing also noted that Microsoft has introduced new risk cohort classifications for how IT and security teams should prioritize vulnerabilities. Dustin Childs , head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day initiative, said CSOs should take action on a hole in SharePoint ( CVE-2026-102866 ), which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. Microsoft said an unauthenticated attacker who obtains a valid proof token for a targeted user could modify the token and submit it to an affected SharePoint server. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to authenticate as that user and access or modify content available to the compromised account. User interaction is not required. A ’monster’ batch of Microsoft fixes There are 55 wormable CVEs this month, Childs warned. These are heavily concentrated across critical infrastructure like DHCP Server (6), Remote Desktop Gateway (3), and Network Policy Server (4). They create “an unprecedented risk of autonomous, network-wide propagation,” he said. “Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception,” commented Childs. “Now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly. It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.” He noted that the volume of CVEs isn’t the real story anymore. “What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs,” he said. “Patch what’s proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal.” Jack Bicer , director of vulnerability research at Action1, drew attention to several critical vulnerabilities that present substantial risks to externally accessible systems and enterprise infrastructure. Windows Message Queuing Queue Manager Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-100202 ), Microsoft PostScript Printer Driver Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-70147 and CVE-2026-70153 ), and Microsoft QUIC Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-105016 and CVE-2026-100219 ) each carry CVSS scores of 9.8 and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication or user interaction. Although active exploitation has not been confirmed for these vulnerabilities, he said, their low attack complexity and potential for severe system compromise make them significant enterprise risks. While one commentator called the number of Microsoft vulnerabilities listed this month as “monster,” Tyler Reguly , Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, disagreed: “I’ve argued that [vulnerability] numbers are meaningless. This month’s number, 1,413, is no different.” There are, however, numbers that hold meaning, he noted. “Twenty-six, for example, is how many 2026 Microsoft CVEs have shown up in the CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] catalogue. Last year, that number was 30, and the year before was 32. That means less than 1% of vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft this year are known to be exploited. That’s an important number, but 1,413 definitely isn’t.” SAP Security Notes In all, SAP released 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to previously released security notes. One, an OAuth2 server-side request forgery vulnerability in SAP Cloud SDK for Python, is rated a 10 in criticality. It affects multi-tenant SAP BTP (Business Technology Platform) applications. An attacker who controls the tenantsubdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated, SAP said . But CSOs with SAP products in their environment will also want to ensure admins have taken action on three other critical vulnerabilities: Security Note 3805589 ( CVE-2026-89107 , with a CVSS score of 9.9) addresses a code injection vulnerability in SAP S/4HANA Manage Substitution/Validation.. This is an app allowing users to display, change, and create substitution and validation rules for selected business contexts and events. These rules can be used in business processes to validate, derive, or replace values at the time of entry for the relevant fields. Jonathan Stross , Pathlock’s senior product manager for cybersecurity R&I, noted that for organizations using these functions for journal-entry rules, the potential consequence is a full compromise of the system that processes those rules. The temporary mitigation also has a business cost, because it prevents users from adding, changing or deleting rules through the related SAP Fiori applications. Fiori is a modern user interface that replaces the traditional SAP interface. To exploit the vulnerability, Stross said, an attacker with the required business-role access needs to submit a malicious rule definition. The vulnerable processing logic treats that input as executable code rather than restricting it to the intended rule language. The resulting risk extends beyond unauthorized changes to an individual substitution or validation rule. No user interaction is required. SAP Security Note 379711 ( CVE-2026-89110 , with a CVSS score of 9.9) patches a broken access control vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. Detected by Onapsis Research Labs (ORL), the issue is that certain portal functionality in Visual Composer allows a low-privileged attacker to invoke internal operations on a preconfigured remote system. A security configuration is available that allows for the definition of an allowlist of permissible data services to be invoked, however, this configuration is not enabled by default. The patch changes the default configuration by enabling the secure settings. The note provides an additional FAQ document and explains how the secure configuration can be enabled manually, prior to applying the permanent patch. A successful exploit of this vulnerability could lead to a full compromise of the remote system. SAP Security Note 3788788 ( CVE-2026-89108 , with a CVSS score of 9.1), patches a missing authorization check vulnerability in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (Configuration Service). Onapsis said that, when authenticated as an SAP XMII Admin user with network access to specific endpoints, an attacker could submit a specially crafted request to provision an account with administrative privileges on the underlying Java application server. This account can be used to fully compromise the system. Adobe security bulletins Adobe released 10 bulletins covering 141 CVEs, reported Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti. Fifteen of these are critical, although Adobe is not aware of exploitation of any of them. Admins should start with the two products holding the most critical severity ratings, he said: ColdFusion (APSB26-144): 10 Critical flaws, including three unauthenticated, network-reachable bugs rated 9.8 or higher (CVE-2026-105899; CVE-2026-106622; and CVE-2026-106624), none of which has as yet been added to the NIST vulnerability database. Users should update to ColdFusion 2025.0.14 or 2023.0.26. Commerce ( APSB26-153 ): five Critical flaws, including CVE-2026-103849 and CVE-2026-92909, neither requiring authentication to exploit. Customers also need to apply the hotfix for CVE-2026-75650 from the September 7 APSB26-146 update.

title: GitLab patches a max-severity regex flaw alongside five high-severity bugs
raw_text: GitLab just fixed a max-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on its servers. The company released a fix on Monday, alongside patches for five other high-severity flaws affecting its source code management and continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) platform. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97229 , was fixed in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 of its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), according to a patch advisory . The company urged administrators of self-managed installations running affected versions to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action, the company said in the advisory. The release also addresses vulnerabilities that could expose protected environment variables, allow unauthorized pipeline execution, and enable attackers to inject crafted content into AI agent instructions. The fixes span both CE and EE, with some issues affecting only the Enterprise Edition. “When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, Helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected,” GitLab added. Critical regex flaw could enable unauthenticated code execution GitLab described CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow issue in the platform’s CI/CD regular expression compiler. Under certain conditions, insufficient validation of regular expressions could have allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server by supplying a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. The vulnerability affects GitLab CE and EE versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. It carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 for potentially allowing remote code execution without authentication, with impacts on confidentiality, integrity, and availability across security boundaries. GitLab credited researcher Johan Carlsson with reporting the flaw through its HackerOne bug bounty program. Pipeline permissions and AI agents in the crosshairs Among the five high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-92883 could allow an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in other users’ browser sessions through a specially crafted repository. The cross-site scripting flaw resulted from improper sanitization of HTML attributes in syntax-highlighted output and carries a CVSS score of 8.7. Two other flaws target pipeline security. CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS 8.5) could have allowed users with the Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches without authorization. CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS 8.2) potentially enabled attackers to poison cached responses for raw repository files, potentially causing targeted pipelines to execute malicious content and access protected environment variables. The remaining issues affect scheduled pipeline execution and GitLab Duo. CVE-2026-81839 (CVSS 7.7) could have allowed authenticated users to run arbitrary pipelines in a transferred project with the new group’s privileges. Another, CVE-2026-96893 (CVSS 7.3), could have allowed an authenticated user to inject crafted content into AI agent instructions, potentially causing unintended command execution attributed to other users. GitLab said it plans to make vulnerability issue details public 90 days after the release in which they were patched. Administrators should therefore prioritize the applicable security updates rather than wait for further technical disclosure. The release also fixes several low-to-medium severity vulnerabilities affecting GitLab Pages, Kubernetes proxying, GraphQL APIs, merge requests, custom roles, the package registry, and repository and project import functions.
summary: GitLab just fixed a max-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on its servers. The company released a fix on Monday, alongside patches for five other high-severity flaws affecting its source code management and continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) platform. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97229 , was fixed in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 of its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), according to a patch advisory . The company urged administrators of self-managed installations running affected versions to upgrade immediately.

title: Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw
raw_text: A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks . Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages. The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned. The issue is now fixed, Bloom Security researcher Golan Myers told CSO. “The npm team confirmed that a fix had been shipped on October 2, introducing a 48-hour expiry for unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations,” he said. Myers said Bloom has not observed active exploitation in the wild, but confirmed that the flaw was successfully used to publish a new version of an existing npm package under their own controlled testing conditions. The fix addresses the exposure associated with unvalidated configurations, although maintainers still need to review their existing trust relationships, Bloom wrote in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Tuesday. A reclaimed repository name enabled package publishing npm’s Trusted Publishing allows package maintainers to publish releases through automated workflows using OpenID Connect (OIDC), avoiding long-lived publishing credentials. However, Bloom found that npm’s trust configuration relied on the GitHub repository’s owner/repository name instead of its immutable repository ID. When a repository is renamed, transferred, or deleted, its former name may become available for another user to claim. An attacker could create a repository at that address and configure a GitHub Actions workflow with the expected filename. Because npm checked the repository name and workflow filename without verifying the permanent repository ID, the attacker could potentially obtain a valid publishing credential for a package they did not own. The researchers demonstrated the attack against a researcher-controlled package, publishing a new version from a GitHub repository belonging to a different organization. The attack did not require compromising the legitimate maintainer’s GitHub or npm account or stealing their credentials. Their registry-wide scan identified more than 1500 vulnerable packages with over 10 million combined downloads and more than one million downloads per month. One package accounted for over 200,000 monthly downloads, according to Bloom. AI agents amplify the supply-chain risk Bloom argues that AI coding agents can accelerate the distribution of malicious dependencies because they increasingly select and install software packages with limited human intervention. Across dozens of organizations, the researchers measured approximately 70 agent-installed packages per endpoint each month, rising to around 350 on developer machines. These figures cover direct installations and exclude transitive dependencies. A malicious release could execute attacker-controlled code through an installation hook when developers or CI systems install the compromised package. AI agents could introduce such a dependency without a developer explicitly selecting it. “A hijacked package doesn’t need to find a developer anymore,” Myers said. “It only needs to be the package an agent chooses.” Apart from GitHub addressing the problem by making unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations expire after 48 hours, npm also tightened its safeguards by rejecting trusted-publishing tokens issued through GitHub Actions’ issue_comment events, alongside the existing restriction on pull_request_target events. Additionally, Bloom recommended that maintainers audit their Trusted Publishing configurations, verify that each trusted repository name still resolves to a repository under their control, and remove and recreate bindings where necessary. The researchers also advised security teams to audit software dependencies and tools used across their environments and enforce controls over what developers and AI agents are permitted to install.
