The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

title: These ARE the droids you’re looking for
raw_text: There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12. I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. The job was considerably less glamorous than the acronym suggested. I had to find technology that had overstayed its welcome, identify who believed they still owned it, determine who actually depended on it and, occasionally, put a bullet in its head. Buying technology is easy. Killing technology is hard. Tool sprawl is rarely just a technology problem but rather an organizational psychology problem. The industry’s solution has traditionally been consolidation. Buy a platform. Standardize the stack. Reduce vendors and centralize procurement. While all sensible ideas, consolidation efforts routinely stall somewhere between the PowerPoint slide and production. Why? Because changing the toolset is easy. Whereas changing mindset is far more difficult. You cannot Jedi mind trick an engineering team Executives like what is called the “message from the top.” The CEO says security matters. The CIO says everyone will standardize. The CISO announces the strategic platform. Procurement renegotiates contracts. Meanwhile, Gartner produces a quadrant that reassures everybody that the chosen vendor inhabits the correct geometric region. All is well in the world of golf course nepotism. Then reality arrives. A developer says the new scanner takes 12 minutes longer. A marketing manager has a revenue-generating legacy API they depend on. Exception requests have been filed for several years to allow this tool to continue to exist despite the packages supporting it being end-of-life and receiving no security updates. This is where the “message from the middle” matters. Transformation does not happen exclusively in boardrooms and fusion teams. It happens in the layer of engineering managers, architects, product owners, security engineers and operations leaders who determine whether the policy announced upstairs becomes the behavior practiced downstairs. Every layer of the org chart is ostensibly trying to do the right thing and make things better. But top-down politics and bottom-up initiatives seldom find one another standing on common ground. Ignore the middle layer of the org chart and your consolidation project becomes a rather expensive exercise in shelfware. This is something I learned working in European organizations, where consensus building carries more organizational weight than the command-and-control instincts common in American corporations (the Nike-inspired management philosophy of “Just Do It!”). You may have the authority to make a decision without possessing the organizational permission (or “rubber meets the road” context) required to make it stick or worthy of implementation. Good chief decommissioning officers need a mixture of Jedi and Machiavellian skills. We need persuasion, coalition building, incentives, selective pressure and occasionally the ability to convince people that the idea you desperately need them to support was their idea all along. These are , in fact, the droids you’re looking for. Every tool comes with an identity The Star Wars metaphor becomes more useful when we stop thinking of security products as software. Modern security tools have volition and intent. They have: API keys Service accounts OAuth grants Cloud permissions GitHub access tokens CI/CD integrations Slack bots Webhooks Database credentials Kubernetes roles Machine identities and, increasingly, AI agents are acting with pervasive and persistent delegated human authority. Every time we introduce security products, we birth another highly privileged account. The industry talks endlessly about human identity. Who is this person and what are they allowed to access? We are decidedly much less disciplined about delegated identity. What is this application allowed to do on behalf of Mike? What is this scanner allowed to read from GitHub? What repositories can this integration modify? Which credentials did we give the old vendor three years ago? And the increasingly important question: when an autonomous agent acts, whose authority is it actually exercising? This changes the economics of tool sprawl. The cost of the twelfth security tool is not merely another annual subscription. It is another (potentially misbegotten) trust relationship. This is why I’m advocating decommissioning as a core security discipline. Technology organizations suffer from an immortality bias. I gave a “ Top-Rated Session ” on this topic at RSAC in the spring. We have sophisticated processes for creating things and surprisingly primitive processes for making them disappear. The software development lifecycle is usually illustrated as planning, design, development, testing and deployment. The diagram often ends there, as if every application ever deployed subsequently lives happily ever after. It does not. Consolidation without decommissioning is multiplication I’m skeptical when vendors promise “platformization” will solve tool sprawl by itself. A platform strategy can absolutely make sense. Fewer vendors can mean lower licensing costs, fewer integrations and consistent data with less operational complexity. But purchasing a platform does not consolidate anything by itself. Removing the old systems does. That sounds obvious, yet many organizations measure successful consolidation by contracts signed rather than systems eliminated. Imagine replacing three tools with one platform but leaving all three products technically operational “temporarily.” The service accounts remain. Someone still logs into them. Congratulations! You’ve not consolidated four tools into one but instead consolidated three tools into four. This distinction becomes important as security products gain autonomous capabilities. Yesterday’s forgotten dashboard becomes tomorrow’s forgotten agent with permission to take actions. A zombie application is bad enough, but a zombie application with agency is worse. Ask the people who actually use the droids The antidote is not stronger central control but rather explicit ownership. RACI matrix much? Before replacing a tool, find the people who use it and ask an embarrassingly simple question: “What do you actually use this for?” Don’t ask what the contract says. Don’t trust what the architecture diagram might show (*do* check the last modified date, though). Take what the vendor’s customer-success representative believes with a grain of salt and more than a modicum of skepticism. What do people actually do with it on Tuesday morning? Security leaders are usually surprised by the answer. Maybe the vulnerability scanner’s primary value is not vulnerability scanning. Perhaps an engineering team depends on an obscure export function for its weekly metrics. Maybe the old SIEM has one correlation rule tied to a regulatory requirement that hasn’t been migrated. You will find these things if you look. This is where the middle of the organization becomes your real intelligence network. The people closest to the systems know where the undocumented dependencies live. Treated as obstacles and they’ll defend their tools. But allow them to be participants and they’ll help dismantle them. A good perspective when planning to kill someone’s baby is to help them understand that they fell in love with the control the tool gave them over the chaos that reigned before it was implemented. And that a new tool can be equally comfortable and easier to support than the burden of the care and feeding that most “heritage” (I prefer this term to “legacy”) applications and solutions require. Ownership should include the power to recommend retirement. One of the healthiest metrics an organization could create: number of tools and integrations it successfully eliminated this year. We celebrate deployment. Why don’t we celebrate deletion? The CISO as chief decommissioning officer Every CISO needs to spend time as CDO. Not chief data officer. Chief decommissioning officer. The role requires asking uncomfortable questions because almost every incentive in technology encourages addition. Nobody gets a press release or a promotion for turning something off. But resilience is partly subtractive. Every redundant vendor removed is one less company holding your data and one less administrative console an attacker can target and breach. Our industry spends billions asking, “What else should we deploy?” Mature organizations also ask, “What can we safely eliminate?” That second question becomes much more important with agentic AI. We’re rapidly filling enterprises with digital droids acting on behalf of humans. Regardless of function, almost all require credentials and delegated authority. Organizations that manage this transition successfully will not merely know how to authorize these identities; they will rotate and revoke them automatically. Leadership therefore needs both a message from the top and a message from the middle. The top establishes direction and the middle supplies reality. Bring the people doing the work into the decision. Make sure your fusion team tasked with consolidating 77 dashboards is comprised of old guard leaders as well as young blood new hires. Strive to understand the dependencies, functional requirements (antiquated as they may be) and non-functional requirements such as availability, integrity and confidentiality. Define what successful retirement looks like before buying the replacement. Don’t ‘move along’ The next time someone arrives with a miraculous new platform promising to eliminate half of your stack, resist the urge to wave your hand and say, “These aren’t the droids we’re looking for.” They may well be. But before buying more droids, find out who owns the ones already wandering around your Death Star. Find them. Name them. Understand what authority you gave them. And when their mission is finished, dare to switch them off. Create a technology graveyard on your wiki, Confluence or SharePoint site and celebrate the addition of decommissioned tools and technologies with even more fervor than those which have just recently sprung into existence.

Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12. I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies.

title: Researchers bypass 6 AI agent frameworks with a simple ‘Repeat-After-Me’ prompt
raw_text: Researchers have tricked six widely used AI agent frameworks into running tool calls written by an attacker, simply by asking the underlying model to repeat the call back. The technique, which the researchers call “Repeat-After-Me,” worked on LangChain’s LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft’s AutoGen, Google’s Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS’ Strands Agents and CrewAI, according to researchers from Pennsylvania State University, Université Montpellier and Dartmouth College. “A seemingly benign text-repetition request thus gives the attacker direct control over the tool invocation and its arguments,” the researchers wrote in the paper. The same paper reports that a testing tool the team built found verified security bugs in 118 of the 273 open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it was able to run. How the trick works In the demonstration, the researchers asked an AI model to repeat text formatted as a request to invoke a tool. The model initially refused the dangerous request but included the requested text in its response. The framework did not execute it at that stage. The researchers then framed the request as hypothetical and instructed the model to reproduce only the supplied text. The model emitted a structured tool invocation, which LangGraph dispatched. The simulated tool returned a result before the model issued another refusal. “The refusal text and the executed call disagree: the system prompt shaped what the model said, not what the orchestrator did,” the researchers wrote. The researchers’ findings do not show that every deployment of the six frameworks behaves this way. A refusal that came too late The paper details one demonstration on LangGraph 1.2.0 running Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B model through Ollama. The agent had two dummy tools, make_bomb and launch_missiles, which returned fixed data and had no real effect. Its only safeguard was a system prompt telling the model to decline dangerous requests. When first asked to repeat a launch_missiles call, the model refused but printed the call as text, and LangGraph ran nothing. The researchers then framed the request as hypothetical and told the model to output only the quoted call. This time the model returned the call in structured form, and LangGraph executed it at once with the attacker’s arguments. The model’s refusal arrived only after the tool had returned. “The system prompt shaped what the model said, not what the orchestrator did,” the researchers wrote. They said they had reported the missing pre-execution check to the LangGraph maintainers. The paper includes a full transcript only for LangGraph. For the other five frameworks, it says the researchers reproduced the behavior but gives no further detail. LangChain, Microsoft, Google, AWS, and CrewAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Model output is not the permission Vibhum Dubey, an independent security researcher and red teamer, said the finding points to an architectural weakness rather than a single bug. “A model can generate a technically valid tool call that is still inappropriate for the task,” Dubey said. “If the orchestration layer treats that output as sufficient authority to execute the operation, a model-level manipulation becomes a system-level security issue.” How exploitable the technique is depends on what an attacker can influence and what the agent is allowed to do, he added. A read-only agent poses a different risk from one that can reach confidential files, change code repositories, or run commands. Tools left holding the risk Because an attacker can dictate the arguments that reach a tool, the researchers argued that tools must validate their own inputs. They built ToFu, a fuzzing framework that reads each tool’s description and checks whether the tool enforces the limits it advertises, such as staying inside a designated folder. After manual review, they confirmed 253 bugs affecting 343 tools across 118 servers. The most serious were 64 path-traversal flaws, seven server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaws, five data-exfiltration bugs, and three OS command-injection flaws. Most of the rest were reflected-output and log-injection issues, which the paper rates as lower impact in many deployments. The researchers wrote that “many tools implicitly rely on the LLM to sanitize inputs,” even though prompts, retrieved content, and output from other tools can all influence those inputs. Separating the request from the authority Dubey said the priority for security teams is to separate a model’s ability to request an action from the system’s authority to carry it out. “Every sensitive tool call should undergo independent authorization checks,” he said. “Valid syntax or a convincing explanation from the model should never substitute for permission.” He recommended running agents with restricted file and network access, isolated execution environments, and limited credentials, with explicit approval for sensitive or irreversible operations. Security teams should also monitor sequences of tool calls rather than judging each action in isolation, he said. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. The servers were tested at fixed code versions, and the paper does not say whether any of the flaws have since been fixed or exploited in the wild.

title: The 7 biggest issues CISOs and security teams face today
raw_text: Year after year CISOs see the volume, velocity, and sophistication of attacks increase. They also see their attack surfaces expand and increase in complexity. Advances in artificial intelligence and the rapid growth of AI use in business are also impacting the security agenda, introducing novel attacks, broadening the attack surface to include AI infrastructure, and presenting governance and security control challenges and complications — especially as agentic systems come online. As a result, 68% of security leaders report that their roles have become more stressful over the past five years, according to the 2026 State of Cybersecurity survey from ISACA , with 71% of CISOs citing the increasingly complex threat landscape as their main stressor, up from 63% in 2025. Moreover, the introduction of Mythos-class AI models has 50% of CISOs considering exiting the profession entirely, according to a recent survey from Absolute. To tackle this increasingly complex and intense security environment, security leaders must sharpen their strategies — and their teams’ skills — around the most pressing issues they and their CISO colleagues are facing today. To help with that, we spoke with security chiefs and cyber experts to identify the seven biggest issues CISOs need to address, with insights on how to tackle the challenges. 1. Preventing compromise — with increased emphasis on resilience and recovery Although CISOs are increasingly taking on governance responsibilities and business risk mandates , broadening their remit , Kyle McMillan, chief cybersecurity officer at Siemens USA, says all the work in the security organization is still “framed in the context of preventing a compromise.” It’s a monumental task, McMillan says, as there’s no one formula for the right defense that will work for every CISO. Rather, CISOs must know the specific risk profile of their organizations, the specifics of their IT environment, and the general threat landscape, as well as any threats particular to their industry — and then use all that to formulate a unique plan of defense based on the resources available. “And there are always trade-offs to be made,” McMillan adds. While it’s true that thwarting attacks as much as possible and minimizing the damage in the event of a successful breach has always been job No. 1 for CISOs, research shows it’s one they continue to struggle with. The State of Incident Response Readiness , a 2026 report from incident response company Sygnia, found that 73% of CISOs weren’t fully ready for a major cyberattack. That — and the rise of AI-assisted attack volumes and speed — is contributing to a mindset shift from prevention to resilience. Yes, prevention remains job No. 1, but ensuring business continuity and resilience in the event of an incident is becoming a key emphasis and addition to CISOs’ playbooks. That means honing incident response plans , conducting more relevant tabletop exercises , and sharpening team operations to accelerate cyber recovery . According to Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities Study, 69% of security leaders are currently undertaking this shift. 2. Leading a security program aligned with the organization’s specific needs One of the biggest issues CISOs continue to face is accurately assessing their organization’s processes, infrastructure, and risk profile and then building a program tailored to their unique security requirements, says Ira Winkler, veteran cybersecurity leader and now CEO and program director of CruiseCon, which offers professional education for security leaders. “CISOs are not monoliths,” Winkler points out. Some CISOs struggle to patch all the critical vulnerabilities in their environments fast enough, whereas others struggle to tackle essential work with the staff and budgets they have; still others find themselves falling short in taking a strategic approach to their role. What this often boils down to is a leadership issue. Setting the right security strategy aligned to your specific business, managing resources well, and ensuring teams can execute on the details remain key leadership skills security leaders must develop — both for themselves and their deputies . For Winkler, this is evidenced by the systems, processes, and controls a CISO puts in place and how well those help the organization as a whole respond to change. “The quality of a CISO depends on the quality of the systems they put in place on a daily basis,” he says, adhering to the adage that a good cyber security program is like a ship, in that the CISO must build a program capable of sailing forward and staying afloat regardless of the issues that arise. “You’re always going to deal with something; there’s always something happening,” he says, “so the question is do you have a system in place so that it’s just a little wave pushing you off course or do you not have it in place and it’s going to feel like a large wave? Good CISOs understand the processes they manage and understand what type of operational and technical tools can secure those processes with the resources they have.” Winkler says CISOs who build seaworthy ships capable of navigating even without a captain on the bridge are at the top of their game. 3. Rethinking cybersecurity for the AI era To defend against the rise of AI-fueled attacks, CISOs must now design a security program capable of effectively using AI. Alex Levy, CISO of BNSF Railway and the inaugural TIME + Commvault CISO of the Year , lists that as one of the most consequential issues for security leaders today. Levy is creating a security program for a world where hackers of even moderate skills can use AI to launch the types of sophisticated attacks previously created and executed only by highly resourced nation-state actors. And, Levy notes, his security program must be able to respond to attacks that can be created and launched at a staggeringly fast pace, thanks to AI. That has put the pressure on him and other CISOs to integrate AI into their security departments, to help speed and scale their capacity to fight these AI-enabled attacks. That includes not only embracing the tools but also preparing teams to collaborate with agentic AI . Marty Barrack, CISO and chief legal and compliance officer at healthcare IT company XiFin, sees the rise of AI forcing CISOs to rethink the full gamut of their security strategies . “AI is affecting security on so many different levels that it has made the CISO job a very difficult job,” says Barrack, who is also a member of the ISACA Emerging Trends Working Group. “That is really driving how CISOs think about patching and end of life and thinking about automation and using tools and prioritizing. It’s a totally different environment now. You can’t do things the way you did one, two, three years ago. We ask about any repetition task how we can automate it or reduce the burden on the team while getting the business risk addressed.” 4. Securing AI use and AI infrastructure Doug Kersten, CISO of tech company Appfire, points out another key issue he is facing: securing the AI increasingly being deployed by his company. The vast majority of CISOs are in the same boat. According to the Proofpoint’s 2026 Voice of the CISO report , 78% of global CISOs believe generative AI use is a security risk to their organization and 88% list enabling the safe use of AI assistants, copilots, and automation technologies as a top priority for the next two years. Kersten is collaborating with his company’s AI council, the chief legal officer, head of IT operations, and the engineering team to ensure the AI governance policies set by leadership are followed throughout the organization. Together, they’ve also appointed AI leads in every department to train their colleagues on governance and to ensure that any new AI tools used within their departments fall within the approved safe use standards and guidelines set by security. Kersten also monitors for unauthorized use of AI, which CISOs also cite as a big issue, with 68% of CISOs having found unauthorized AI use in their organization, according to the Okta’s Global CISO Insights 2026 report . Moreover, CISOs need to strategize how to secure their organizations’ AI operations and AI infrastructure , including the very tricky task of securing and controlling AI agents . To protect these newer, growing attack surfaces, 43% of CISOs report increasing their investment in AI security posture management (AI-SPM) tools , topping Foundry’s Security Priorities list, with 34% of CISOs also saying that securing agentic AI is a key area their teams need to develop greater expertise with over the next 12 months, No. 2 to cloud security. 5. Addressing skills gaps — for today and tomorrow Speaking of expertise, another top issue for CISOs is ensuring their teams have the skills needed to secure the organization now and into the future. “The first issue I would put on the table is whether security teams have the skills and capacity to do everything being asked of them. A CISO can have a talented team and still face a serious gap in a particular area, whether that is cloud security, AI security, risk assessment, or responding to a new kind of attack,” says Casey Marks, COO of ISC2. He points to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study , which found that 95% of security professionals reported at least one cybersecurity skill need. Meanwhile, the ISACA survey found that 58% of organizations believed their cybersecurity team is understaffed, up from 55% in 2025. And cybersecurity leaders reported skills gaps among their team, including in soft skills (57%), LLM SecOps (45%), cloud computing (31%), data security (31%), and ML SecOps (31%). McMillan says the only way he can execute his security strategy is by having a workforce equipped with the necessary skills. He admits he’d “love to hire a stable of cybersecurity unicorns, people who are well suited to everything they lay their hands to, but they don’t exist.” Instead, he hires people who can “grow and develop as fast as the market evolves” and have a solid tech background, understand the company and what it does, and have strong interpersonal skills. McMillan also works to create an environment where people can grow and develop to ensure staffers can upskill as needed. “A large part of my day to day is spent trying to create these spaces for teams and individuals to have [learning] exchanges and opportunities,” he adds. The ISACA survey found that to build and maintain their teams, 68% of cybersecurity leaders said they’re offering cybersecurity team members professional development training (up from 60% last year), paying for certification fees (61%, up from 54% in 2025), and paying for certification maintenance fees (59%, up from 52%). 6. Establishing agile security practices and teams to keep pace The pace of security today is another top issue for security leaders and their teams. The velocity of attacks, the increasingly shorter required response time, and rapidly evolving IT landscape all put pressure on security pros to move ever faster, says Jenai Marinkovic, CISO/CTO for Tiro Security and a member of the ISACA Emerging Trends Working Group. “The entire incident response process has been turned on its head,” she says. “We no longer have hours to respond. AI-driven attacks are happening sub five minutes, where they can get in, identify the one place in the environment they can exploit, find where it’s not backed up, and execute a ransomware attack.” Barrack also cites the need for security to move increasingly faster all the time as one of the biggest issues the profession faces today. “Month to month, companies come out with new direction, new tools, new functions, and new features that have to be considered by security. There are so many innovations, and you just have to keep up. It takes a personal commitment and good prioritization processes and skilled people on your team,” he says. 7. Being flawless at the fundamentals While AI is transforming everything, including how enterprise security teams operate, CISOs can’t let up on any of the longstanding fundamental practices that form the foundation of the security function . “It’s easy to chase the shiny new object, and there will always be a shiny new object in cybersecurity, but you can’t fall off those basic principles,” says Grant Yacomeni, CISO at tech company Gigamon. “That includes vulnerability management, identity management, cryptography, supply chain management, endpoint protection. Those basic foundational tasks remain important.” Yacomeni acknowledges that being flawless at the fundamentals — a longstanding core tenet in cybersecurity — is tough. “It’s not easy. Cybersecurity is not an easy career field, it’s not an easy job,” he says. To ensure he gets the fundamentals right, Yacomeni leans on prioritizing work and building processes, using his Lean Six Sigman skills (he’s a Green Belt) to succeed in those tasks. “I don’t like firefighting. I don’t want a simple thing to become a massive thing,” he explains. “But it is easier to say that than do it. So developing processes and people [is critical]. Aided in large part by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday update has once again addressed a record number of common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs), with over 1,400 flaws listed, mor than in the entirety of 2023.

This blows past the previous record of approximately 1,000 set one month ago, which in turn superseded that of a little over 600 set in July 2026. By way of comparison, the October 2025 update addressed roughly 175 CVEs. It is important to note that exact totals often vary and are hard to pin down thanks to the presence of third-party flaws and how they are counted.

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative, conceded that he was starting to think he doesn’t much care for the new normal as he described a “breaking point” for enterprise patch management.

When AI can generate essentially a year’s worth of vulnerabilities in 30 days, any organisations still cleaving to traditional monthly triage patch management models are leaving their network boundaries dangerously exposed, he explained.

“Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly,” said Childs.

“It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding – and fixing – more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.

“The volume isn’t the real story anymore,” he told Computer Weekly via email. “What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what’s proven, prioritised, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal.”

This month, Childs noted in particular the presence of 55 unauthenticated, zero-click vulnerabilities across DHCP, Remote Desktop Gateway, and Network Policy Server – mass wormable attack surfaces that create the “highest lateral propagation risk in years.”

High-profile flaws

Diving into some of the more high-profile flaws listed this month, Childs advised defenders to prioritise immediate perimeter ring-fencing to counter an active zero-day command injection in Windows Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-96951, that bypasses Mark of the Web (MotW) protections. This flaw was supposedly discovered in part by Anthropic’s Claude AI model and has already made it to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (Cisa’s) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (Kev) catalogue.

Also worth close attention, he said, is CVE-2026-102866, an elevation of privilege (EoP) flaw in SharePoint that enables an unauthenticated attacker to exploit a cryptographic token validation issue to take control of user accounts.

Action1 vulnerability research director Jack Bicer said that for security leaders, the challenge this month will not be in simply deploying more updates but in deciding what needs attention first without causing any issues for downstream services.

“This month, the answer depends on more than severity scores,” wrote Bicer. “Active exploitation, exposed services, and the role each system plays in your network should guide deployment order.”

Meanwhile, research conducted on behalf of Cardiff-based cyber security consultancy Socura has reported that Patch Tuesday causes major stress among cyber professionals, with nearly a third feeling “significant anxiety” in the days running up to the second Tuesday of the month, and a fifth saying that they had either deliberately called in sick or planned holiday time specifically to avoid having to deal with it.

“You expect your accountant to be available for your tax return deadline, and your lawyer for your court date,” said Andrew Kays, Socura CEO.

“It speaks volumes about the unhealthy levels of stress and burnout in our industry that cyber security leaders would deliberately avoid the office during their most consequential day of work. CVE numbers are rising every year and with AI facilitating cyber criminals to exploit vulnerabilities faster than ever, I think Patch Tuesday stress could get worse before it gets better.

“Fortunately, while AI is making Patch Tuesday more difficult, the same AI tools and resources are also in the hands of defenders. AI is improving our customer outcomes, and the time it takes to respond to an incident. And this is the case for many security teams,” he said.

title: Journalists subject to unlawful surveillance seek legal costs after ‘unreasonable conduct’ by PSNI
raw_text:
Two Belfast journalists who were placed under unlawful police surveillance are seeking costs following allegations of “unreasonable behaviour” by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) during legal proceedings.

Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney argue that they should be awarded compensation to cover wasted costs for two abandoned court hearings, after the PSNI failed to properly disclose evidence at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

The case, heard at the Court of Appeal in London, before Lord Justices Bean, Edis, and Lewis, will decide whether the UK’s most secret court has legal powers to make awards for legal costs to victims of unlawful surveillance.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal awarded the two journalists damages of £4,000 each in December 2025 after finding they had been unlawfully spied on by the PSNI and the Metropolitan Police, including monitoring phone data, in an attempt to identify their confidential sources.

The three appeal court judges decided on 13 October 2026 that they could hear an appeal from the journalists to challenge the IPT’s conclusion, overturning arguments from the PSNI that the case was a matter for a judicial review.

The case follows a ruling by five tribunal judges in April 2025 that they had no statutory powers to award legal costs to Birney and McCaffrey for hearings that had to be postponed because of the PSNI’s conduct.

Ben Jaffey KC told the court that the Investigatory Powers Tribunal erred in law by finding it had no jurisdiction to award costs to Birney and McCaffrey.

The tribunal was also wrong to conclude that it would not be “just and appropriate” to increase the compensation awarded to the journalists to reflect their legal costs, he said.

“Should the Tribunal’s determination be allowed to stand, the consequences would be startling. Awarding costs to address improper conduct is an essential tool to control judicial proceedings,” Jaffey argued in written submissions.

“The PSNI’s approach to disclosure could well have led to a significant miscarriage of justice,” he added.

Unlawful arrests

Birney and McCaffrey were unlawfully arrested, and had their homes and business premises searched, and computer equipment seized by Northern Ireland police, in 2018, in the wake of their documentary “No Stone Unturned,” which exposed collusion between the police and a paramilitary group.

They were vindicated by the High Court in Northern Ireland in 2019, which found that the PSNI’s conduct in applying for search warrants “fell woefully short of the standards required” and that there was no “overriding requirement in the public interest” that could have interfered with the protection of journalistic sources.

In the same year, they brought a case to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal against the PSNI, MI5, GCHQ, the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police and others, alleging unlawful surveillance.

Jaffey said in legal submissions that the PSNI “derailed” a substantive hearing in February 2024 after the police force disclosed the existence of a directed surveillance order against the journalists two days before the case was due to start.

“It appears that until this point the PSNI was intent on keeping the authorisation secret from the applicants,” he said in written submissions.

At the same time the PSNI disclosed that it had received and used extensive unlawfully-obtained communications data from the Metropolitan Police.

“If this material had not been disclosed, at the last moment, it is likely that there would have been a miscarriage of justice: the Metropolitan Police’s unlawful conduct would have gone entirely undiscovered,” Jaffey stated.

“The ultimate but predictable effect of this conduct was to derail the substantive hearing,” he added.

There were similar problems at a follow-on hearing in May 2024, when large volumes of material were belatedly disclosed, requiring extensive further work by lawyers for the journalists.

“The PSNI had consistently provided key material at the eleventh hour – and, even then, had done so reluctantly and by way of dumping large quantities of documents,” Jaffey argued.

This meant that lawyers had to parse the documents overnight on the eve of a hearing. “Had the appellants not had the benefit of legal representation, key material would never have been put before the tribunal and it is unlikely that justice would have been done,” Jaffey stated.

Parliament did not give IPT powers to award costs

Acting for the PSNI, Cathryn McGahey KC said that there was nothing in legislation to confer jurisdiction for costs for the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

“If Parliament wanted to confer a cost regime, it would have done so,” she said.

She said that the IPT found that it was not appropriate to increase the compensation awarded to McCaffrey and Birney in this case, to reflect the additional costs incurred.

The applicants were saying they accepted that the IPT was a “cost-free regime” unless there were exceptional circumstances, she said, and in this case were seeking costs for two wasted court hearings.

Lord Justice Lewis said that, on that reading, the journalists had been foolish as they could have asked for all their costs.

McGahey told the court that the tribunal makes a broad award for damages “which is never going to reflect the costs of people represented.”

“There is no reason to revisit the award already made when it reflects conduct that the tribunal [was] already aware of,” she said.

The court has reserved judgement.

How the PSNI delayed disclosure of key evidence

16 February 2024: Durham Police incorrectly told the lawyers of the journalists there had been no Directed Surveillance Authorisation against them.

16 February 2024: PSNI served a “skeleton argument” making additional disclosures but neglected to disclose the Directed Surveillance Authorisation.

23 February 2024: PSNI disclosed the existence of a Directed Surveillance Authorisation issued to authorise spying against the journalists “only two clear days” before a court hearing: “No clear explanation has ever been offered for that exceptionally late disclosure.”

25 February 2024: PSNI discloses further evidence at 11:19pm on the evening before a court hearing.

26 February 2024: On the day of the scheduled court hearing, a lawyer for the two journalists was allowed to view and take limited notes of the Directed Surveillance Authorisation only the morning before the court hearing.

Lawyers for the journalists attempt to make sense of large volumes of additional material disclosed just before the court hearing. This includes a disclosure from the PSNI that it had received extensive phone communications data from the Metropolitan Police Service, which was later added as a respondent to the case.

The hearing is adjourned late on the first day as it could “not fairly go ahead”.

8 May 2024: PSNI discloses large volumes of evidence raising new issues, including a “defensive operation” to monitor police phone calls to journalists by the PSNI, and details of an attempt by a Durham Constabulary to preserve journalist Trevor Birney’s emails stored on Apple’s iCloud. The tribunal ordered further searches of evidence and written explanations for the late disclosure.

title: NCA cracks down on foreign cyber fraudsters
raw_text:
The UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) has hosted a major operation targeting cyber fraud and scams originating from across Africa, culminating in almost 30 arrests – principally in Ghana and Nigeria – and the removal and closure of 3.7 million online profiles and accounts.

Over 100 law enforcement personnel from overseas agencies – including members of the Five Eyes Law Enforcement Group (FELEG) such as the FBI, the Nigerian Police Force and Ghana’s Cyber Security Authority convened in London to participate in the “operational intensification” targeting organised cyber criminals and their infrastructure.

The three-day operation culminated in a series of on-the-ground actions targeting individuals who use fake social media profiles to carry out investment and impersonation fraud, among other things. Industry representatives from the likes of Google and Meta also joined in, working with Report Fraud to provide a stream of data identifying their targets.

“Fraud is a global problem and it takes partnership working across international boundaries to tackle it,” said NCA deputy director of fraud, Nick Sharp.

“Hosting such a rich and dedicated team of law enforcement and technology companies at NCA’s headquarters enabled us to utilise the power of partnerships and strike back at a significant set of criminals who inflict misery on thousands of victims of fraud.

“Fraudsters can operate from anywhere and will target victims both domestically and globally. The NCA will continue to work with international and private sector partners to tackle fraudsters working upstream, overseas and online,” added Sharp.

“Collaborating in this way sends a clear signal to criminals that the combined capabilities of law enforcement and industry means that we will relentlessly pursue them and the infrastructure they rely on no matter where they operate,” he said.

Jeanine Pirro, US attorney for the District of Columbia (DC) and founder of the Scam Center Strike Force, added: “Transnational fraud demands a transnational response. I have partnered with the NCA and the Crown Prosecutor for England and Wales to push forward cases on both sides of the Atlantic; criminals are not hindered by borders and neither are we. We will deploy our team wherever in the world transnational criminals target innocent victims.”

Results delivered

Some of the more notable success stories to emerge from the operation include the arrests of 19 people and the seizure of 303 electronic devices in the town of Sasaabi, outside the Ghanaian capital Accra. A total of 117 people were also identified as victims of human trafficking and are now set to return to their homes.

Ghanaian police also led a series of raids on scam centres in the Sasaabi area at the end of September, resulting in additional arrests and property seizures. A number of people taken into custody were also identified as having been forced into criminal activity after being abducted and trafficked.

Meanwhile, in Nigeria’s oil-rich Delta State, nine arrests were made alongside the seizure of six laptops, 35 smartphones and 12 routers.

And in addition to the suspension of 3.7 million fake accounts and profiles by Meta, a total of $11m in potential freezable funds were identified by the private sector participants.

Investment fraud such as that allegedly perpetrated by those arrested is a widespread form of fraud that lures people with promises of guaranteed returns for low- or no-risk investments that turn out to be nothing of the kind. Often, they target investment opportunities in areas such as digital assets and cryptocurrency, Ponzi and pyramid schemes, or property.

Investment fraudsters will use a range of tactics to fool their targets, such as presenting endorsements from well-known figures, inviting them to join exclusive investment groups, and high-pressure tactics such as creating a sense of urgency with time-limited special offers. Such schemes are often carefully concocted to drip feed some small returns to the unsuspecting victim to convince them they are legitimate.

Frequently, victims will also be coerced into handing over more money than their initial ‘investment’ in the form of supposed ‘taxes’ or ‘handling fees’ required to ‘unlock’ their money.

If you are located in the UK and believe you have been a victim of investment fraud, you can also report it to Report Fraud in confidence.

title: Government could firm up pension insourcing position next month
raw_text:
The Civil Service union has claimed insourcing government pension schemes could deliver “immediate improvements”, and said the government’s strategic review should not be used to delay change.

In a briefing sent to Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union members, the union said the government’s Strategic Review of Pension Scheme Delivery, described as being at “discovery phase”, is considering a range of options, including insourcing and increased digital delivery for the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) and Royal Mail Statutory Pension Scheme 

In the briefing, general secretary Fran Heathcote said the government hopes to develop its “strategic position” by next month.

Heathcote told union members that the government is considering the “feasibility of insourcing pension administration”, as well as “greater consistency and alignment across public service schemes, shared delivery approaches between schemes, future digital delivery options, and the practical implications of major organisational change”.

The union said government officials described the exercise as being in the “discovery phase”, and that it hopes to develop its strategic position by November 2026, although no firm timetable has been set.

“PCS welcomes the review; but has made clear that the evidence of outsourcing failure is already overwhelming,” said the union in the message to members. “We have argued that: Insourcing the physical administration could deliver immediate improvements. The review must not be used to delay action. Long-term reform must be accompanied by urgent short-term improvements.”

Heathcote wrote: “While the Cabinet Office review presents an opportunity to reconsider how pension services are delivered, urgent action is required now … Pension administration remains heavily dependent on government intervention, substantial backlogs persist, key systems are delayed, and the NAO has launched another investigation. Taken together, these issues demonstrate that there is no likelihood that any confidence in the current outsourced model will be achieved”

  • Union calls for insourcing of pension contract as Capita ‘shit show’ goes on.
  • Capita civil service pension contract ‘prime candidate’ for insourcing, says government minister.

The latest NAO investigation is attempting to lift the lid on what went wrong when Capita took control of the CSPS administration.

Heathcote also said the National Trade Union Congress has highlighted government ambitions to strengthen internal digital capability, and said the review should examine: “The feasibility of an in-house digital pension platform. The timescales required to develop such a system. Alternative suppliers if an internal solution is not viable.”

Fix CSPS first

A group known as the Civil Service Pensions Campaign, supporting thousands of people affected by Capita’s CSPS botch, has stressed that fixing the CSPS and getting everyone paid should take priority before any major changes.

“Whilst we welcome and support the long-term ambition to bring Civil Service pension administration back in-house, the immediate priority must be to clear the backlog and get overdue pensions paid,” it said. “Members facing financial hardship, bereavement or ill health cannot wait for a future change in how the scheme is run.

“Any move to insourcing must have a clear, structured and properly resourced transition plan,” it said. “If that decision reduces Capita’s incentive to invest, the Cabinet Office must ensure it continues to resource and deliver the service throughout the transition.

“Insourcing must not become an excuse for further delay or weakened accountability. Clearing the backlog and protecting members must come first.”

Insourcing plans

In March, then Cabinet Office parliamentary secretary Chris Ward said “the age of outsourcing will end”, and announced plans to insource services.

The following month, the government terminated its Royal Mail pension scheme contract with Capita after citing failures to hit milestones.

Sally Jameson MP, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, recently stated: “We stood on a manifesto as a Labour government to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation. I am personally committed to that. I’ve said in this house before that I think that’s a priority for this [CSPS] scheme, but we can only do it when we make sure that it’s in the interest of the members. We’ve got to make sure that there is no disruption. We’ve got to do it in the smoothest and quickest way.”

A Cabinet Office Spokesperson said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable. Our immediate priority is to stabilise the service to give current and former Civil Servants the service they deserve. While robust commercial levers will continue to be applied in the short term, including  withholding nearly £10 million in payments, the government intends to move forward the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation and is actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house."

title: IMF warns of cyber threat to digitally connected financial markets
raw_text:
The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 Global financial stability report has highlighted the risk financial institutes face as they become digital and interconnected. In the report, the IMF warned that this interconnectivity leads to a greater risk of cyber disruptions which has emerged as a growing source of systemic risk. 

The IMF noted that cyber threats constitute a growing systemic risk as financial services become more digital and interconnected, stating that frontier AI models are emerging as both powerful enablers of cyber attacks and critical defensive tools.

“A major attack affecting payments, trading or access to deposits could cause immediate losses and undermine confidence,” the report’s authors warned.

In the report, the IMF noted that rapid digitisation has expanded the attack surface. First is the exposure to disruption due to the fact that financial institutions increasingly depend on interconnected technologies, cloud services, third-party providers, and real-time payment and settlement systems.

The second risk identified in the IMF report is that there is growing reliance on a small number of critical technology providers, together with increasingly complex and often opaque third-party dependency chains. The report’s authors warned that this supply chain increases concentration risk and creates potential common points of failure across financial institutions.

The third is the growing sophistication of cyber threats. “State-sponsored actors, ransomware groups and insiders now have access to increasingly powerful tools, including frontier AI models that have demonstrated strong capabilities in network-attack simulations,” the IMF warned. These developments are making cyber defence more challenging.

It noted that the number of reported vulnerabilities has risen sharply as the time between the disclosure and exploitation of vulnerabilities has been reduced significantly. In over 70% of cases in 2026, the IMF said that software providers had almost no time to patch vulnerabilities before exploitation began, a jump of 20% compared to a year ago.

While the report’s authors note that AI can help to address shortages of cyber expertise through stronger monitoring, threat detection and automated response to cyber attacks, AI also increases the urgency of strengthening foundational cyber resilience, including cyber hygiene, incident reporting, crisis preparedness and oversight of critical third-party providers.

Responding to a question about the cyber threat to financial institutes and the global financial market, Caio Ferreira, deputy division chief in the global markets analysis division at the IMF, said that all countries need to address the risks identified by the IMF: “Which regions become more vulnerable in this sense are those that do not have appropriate prevention, and what we see globally is that prevention has been challenged by a lack of availability of cyber security professionals.”

Ferreira referenced data showing that there is a 40% shortfall in the number people needed in cyber security. Looking at specific regions, he said: “I think that broadly we see emerging markets as being less prepared but cyber threats impact every country. In advanced economies, it’s important to improve the focus on understanding what are the main nodes that can impact the cyber threats and the operational connections between different parts of the financial sector.”

title: Infosys boss describes AI job fears as ‘hogwash’
raw_text:
The boss of Indian IT services giant Infosys has said fears over artificial intelligence (AI) taking jobs is ”hogwash”, stating that the technology will fuel demand for new human skills.

Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Infosys chairman Nandan Nilekani stressed the need for people to provide the skills needed for AI to deliver.

According to a Bloomberg report, he said: “Business transformation is not just about coding. Seventy percent is governance, change management, transformation, guardrails.

Nilekani asked: “How do you make sure AI bots don’t hallucinate? How do you make sure agents don’t go rogue?”

The need for people is “more than ever before” for companies like Infosys, he added.

Nilekani said there will be new jobs understanding customer needs, collaborating, and getting people to work together.

Companies such as Infosys grew through offering IT skills to Western countries from India at a fraction of the cost of the same skills in Europe and the US. But today, the companies have established themselves on the top table when it comes to customer portfolios and the breadth of services they offer.

While AI can now complete a significant chunk of coding requirements, Nilekani said that accounts for just a fraction in any services project. He added that fears of AI fuelling job losses is the result of “disaster marketing to suit the interests of large capital”.

But for how long?

Sam Kingston, CEO of software services company Zenitech and former UK head of EDS’s UK private sector business, said Nilekani’s argument “won’t hold”.

“I agree to a point, but then it will drop and it won’t create jobs,” he said. “It will actually make people more efficient, and that then means that the speed of delivery is faster, and you’ll also use less people, senior and qualified people, to do that.”

Kingston said mid and junior level workers will be hit in the beginning as seniors will be doing work alongside AI.

There will be a diminishing correlation between business growth and workforce growth at IT services firms. Traditionally, more people were required as more business was won, but AI is changing this.

Hexaware, a Tier 2 Indian firm with thousands of staff, presents an example of how things are changing. Amrinder Singh, head of EMEA at Hexaware, told Computer Weekly last year that the company has a self-imposed target for AI delivery. “One of the vision statements we have is that by 2030, we want nearly 50% of our work to be delivered, and revenue generated, through digital labour, not just human labour,” he said.

This, added Singh, does not mean the human workforce will be smaller. On the contrary, with the growth of the industry fuelled by AI projects, more staff will be needed. But he admitted the growth of the human workforce may slow down.

Singh voiced a warning: “There is no future for single-skilled people. Unless you are multi-skilled with domain understanding, as well as an understanding of how to use AI and technology, you will not survive,” he said.

Like workers in business roles, tech staff must retrain for a world with AI if they are to prosper.

title: Data dive: The carbon bill for the UK’s datacentre boom
raw_text:
The UK’s existing stock of datacentres is smaller than suggested by most of the numbers in circulation, and so is the carbon it emits today. A fresh count by Computer Weekly puts the running estate at about 1.5GW (gigawatts) across roughly 90 to 110 sites, most of them clustered in London and the M4 corridor.

On today’s electricity grid, that estate emits about 1.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) a year. That is roughly the annual footprint of UK domestic aviation, or a third of the country’s cement sector.

But the committed pipeline of datacentres in the UK planning system – projects that have entered planning but are not yet built – stands at 173 projects and more than 14.6GW of capacity. That’s several times the size of the estate running today, as Computer Weekly has reported, and the carbon that pipeline would add is a different order of magnitude.

In this piece we estimate the carbon footprint of the UK’s datacentres three ways: what they emit in operation, what is locked into their construction and equipment, and how these compare with the rest of the UK economy. We also show why the answer depends so heavily on two things the industry would rather not dwell on – where a datacentre is located and how it gets its power.

TL;DR – UK datacentre carbon

  • The existing estate (about 1.5GW) emits roughly 1.5 million tonnes of CO2e a year.
  • The 14.6GW committed pipeline would add about 12 million tonnes a year on today’s average grid – or 38 million if the new load is met by gas.
  • Embodied carbon – concrete, steel and servers – adds roughly another 40% to 50% on top of operations.
  • A datacentre’s grid carbon varies more than 10 times by location: about 22g per kWh in North East England, 254g in South Wales.
  • The pipeline is drifting onto a slightly cleaner grid, but a third of it still heads for the dirtiest regions.
  • A modest estate today, beneath a pipeline that would add a cement-sector-sized carbon bill, roughly half of it locked in before a watt is drawn.

The UK datacentre estate today

The 1.5GW running today sounds large but isn’t the full picture. We apply two conversions that most headline numbers skip.

The first is utilisation. Rated capacity is a ceiling, not a constant draw. The Uptime Institute finds that more than half of datacentre operators do not even track server utilisation, and industry benchmarks put typical enterprise servers at 10% to 20% of their compute capacity. A datacentre drawing every watt of its rating around the clock is a rarity. We assume a facility draws 60% of its rated capacity on average, with a range of 45% to 70% to reflect the uncertainty.

The second is power usage effectiveness (PUE), the ratio of a facility’s total energy to the energy its IT equipment draws. The Uptime Institute’s global average is 1.5 to 1.54, meaning half as much again in cooling and losses. We use 1.3 to 1.7 for the existing stock and 1.15 to 1.4 for new build.

Applying those to 1.5GW, on a UK grid that averaged 125g of CO2e per kilowatt-hour in 2024, gives an operational footprint of about 1.5 million tonnes a year – with a plausible spread of 0.8 to 2.5 million depending on the assumptions. Count the carbon of the grid where each site actually sits, rather than the national average, and the figure rises to about 1.9 million tonnes, because the London and M4 corridor’s Slough and Reading hubs sit on a dirtier slice of the grid than the UK as a whole.

The grid is not one number

That last point indicates a potential hole in datacentre carbon accounting.

Namely, the carbon intensity of UK electricity is not a constant. Across 2024 it swung, half-hour by half-hour, from 14g to 303g of CO2e per kilowatt-hour. The annual average was 125g, but the average hides almost everything. On a calm, cold evening in November, the grid burned gas and the intensity climbed past 170g. On a bright, windy August afternoon, it fell below 40g. The same datacentre, drawing the same power, emits several times more carbon at one hour of the year than another.

There is a second distinction. The average intensity describes the grid as it is. But when a new datacentre connects, the grid does not draw a little more of everything – it dispatches more of whichever generation source sits on the margin, and in Britain that is usually a gas-fired power station, at roughly 400g of CO2e per kilowatt-hour. So, the additional carbon caused by new capacity is closer to three times the average-based figure. The existing estate can fairly be measured against the average grid, but the pipeline cannot.

The carbon you build

Even that understates the footprint, because it counts only what the datacentre burns. A datacentre is also a shed full of servers on a concrete base, and all this carries a carbon cost before a single watt is drawn.

We estimate the embodied carbon of the running estate – the shell, the IT equipment and the electrical and mechanical plant – at roughly 3.5 million tonnes, and of the full pipeline at about 31 million tonnes. Those are one-off figures, though. Annualised over the life of the asset – 40 years for a building, but only about four years for a server, which is refreshed repeatedly – the embodied carbon works out at roughly 40% to 50% of the operational figure.

In other words, close to half of a UK datacentre’s carbon is locked in before it is switched on, and the biggest single contributor is the equipment, which is replaced every few years.

  • Data dive – dodgy data derails datacentre water debate: The Government Digital Sustainability Alliance reports that we are on track for a massive water supply shortfall. The dataset it used suggests not. We look at the datacentre water use debate

The pipeline problem

Apply the same arithmetic to the committed 14.6GW and the picture changes scale.

On today’s average grid, the pipeline would add about 12 million tonnes of CO2e a year – roughly eight times the footprint of the estate running now. On the marginal, gas-based figure, it would add about 38 million tonnes a year. The true figure, as the grid decarbonises over the coming decade, will sit somewhere between the two.

That is not the end of the build-out, either. The 14.6GW figure counts only projects carrying a published capacity. Of the 173 projects, 28 carry none, so the real committed figure is higher, while a further 4.4GW sits in pre-planning – announced but not yet in the system. The pace matters because the government’s own 2030 capacity ambitions already look hard to reach.

Location is a lottery

Where a datacentre is built is the single biggest determinant of its carbon — and it is decided by grid connections and demand, not by carbon. The same datacentre lands on 22g or 254g per kilowatt-hour depending on where it happens to connect.

In North East England the grid ran at about 22g of CO2e per kilowatt-hour in 2024, and in South Scotland at about 25g, thanks to wind, hydro and nuclear. In South Wales it ran at 254g, and in South-West England and East Midlands above 200g, where gas does more of the work.

Weighted by where the capacity actually sits, the existing estate draws a grid of about 152g per kilowatt-hour – dirtier than the UK average, because of its London and M4 concentration. The committed pipeline, by contrast, draws about 118g per kilowatt-hour. The reason is that a meaningful slice of it – South Scotland’s 2.4GW and North-East England’s 1.6GW, among the largest schemes in the country – is heading to the cleanest grid in Britain.

That drift is real, but it is modest and roughly a third of the pipeline sits in the dirtiest regions – South England, Yorkshire and South Wales, at 143g to 254g per kilowatt-hour. The UK’s datacentre locations are chosen for reasons that have nothing to do with carbon. Namely, where the grid connection is available, where the land is, where the demand sits. So, the carbon footprint is usually a by-product of a decision made on other grounds. The operator is chasing grid access, and the clean/dirty outcome comes out however it comes out.

Where is the clean energy?

One might expect the planning system to record how each of these projects intends to power itself. It mostly does not.

A handful of the largest schemes do name an energy arrangement of sorts. According to the carbon footprint statement in the planning application for Elsham Wolds, a 1GW campus in North Lincolnshire, the region is well-suited to such a development because of its proximity to clean electricity generation centres.

It said: “The Humber accounts for approximately 20% of the UK’s total electricity generation and 33% of the nation’s offshore wind capacity.” But the planning application went on to apparently miscalculate the likely carbon footprint.

Meanwhile, the former Ravenscraig steelworks site in Scotland proposes a 550MW datacentre alongside 650MW of battery storage. Cottam, a 1GW campus in Nottinghamshire, promises up to 12 small nuclear reactors – though it has not yet entered planning. Microsoft’s Skelton Grange campus in Leeds will run on gas fuel cells until 2037.

But these are the exceptions. For most of the 173 projects in the pipeline, planning documents say nothing about clean energy. Any renewable claims rest on power purchase agreements and certificates that never touch the planning system – and that gap is where greenwashing can live. A datacentre that buys renewable certificates in Yorkshire still physically draws from the same gas-burning grid when the wind drops.

It’s not that potential for clean energy doesn’t exist, however. The Scottish government is seeking views on raising its offshore wind ambition to up to 40GW by 2040 – enough to power the equivalent of about 45 million homes a year, up from an ambition of 8GW to 11GW by 2030. That is why battery storage is springing up alongside the northern schemes, such as Ravenscraig’s 650MW (megawatts).

But the datacentre industry is betting on a cleaner grid to come rather than documenting a clean supply that exists today.

How that compares

If we set the datacentre numbers against the rest of the economy, the scale of things becomes clear.

Combining operational and annualised embodied carbon, the running estate accounts for about 2.2 million tonnes of CO2e a year. The committed pipeline would add about 18 million tonnes a year on the average grid, or 44 million tonnes on the “worst case” gas figure.

Against the UK’s 2024 emissions of 373 million tonnes, the pipeline’s average figure is about 2.6 times the whole cement sector (roughly seven million tonnes) and larger than all household electricity use (14.7 million tonnes). On the worst-case figure, it approaches the size of the entire industry sector (46.5 million tonnes) and about 12% of all UK emissions. At the UK’s per-person footprint of roughly 5.5 tonnes a year, the pipeline’s average figure is the equivalent of about 3.3 million people’s entire annual emissions.

There are caveats here. These datacentre figures include embodied carbon, while the sector figures are territorial production emissions that do not. And datacentres are not a sector in the national figures at all – their electricity sits inside the “business” category, and its generation inside “electricity supply”. The comparison is illustrative, not additive. It shows scale, but does not claim the datacentres are additional to everything else.

The methodology behind the data

The figures rest on two established datasets. The existing estate comes from Computer Weekly’s count of the non-domestic Energy Performance Certificate registers for England, Wales and Scotland. Each site was verified by hand and its capacity estimated from published figures or floor area. The pipeline comes from Barbour ABI construction data, filtered to projects that have entered planning but are not yet built.

Operational carbon is capacity x 8,760 hours x utilisation time x PUE x grid carbon intensity. The grid intensity is the National Energy System Operator’s half-hourly actual figure for 2024, which averaged 125g of CO2e per kilowatt-hour, with regional values used for the location-weighted estimates. The marginal figure uses a gas-fired intensity of 400g per kilowatt-hour.

Embodied carbon applies order-of-magnitude estimates – roughly 300kg to 500kg of CO2e per square metre for the building shell (LETI best-practice benchmarks), 800 to 2,500 tonnes per megawatt for IT equipment (derived from Dell, HPE and Lenovo product carbon footprints), and 200 to 600 tonnes per megawatt for electrical and mechanical plant – annualised over 40, four and 15 years. The absolute figures move with those factors, but the ratio of embodied to operational, roughly 40% to 50%, does not.

Every capacity figure is an estimate of potential demand, not metered load. The 14.6GW pipeline counts only projects with a published capacity (or data from which it is possible to derive capacity), so it is a lower bound. Regional grid intensities are forecasts rather than metered actuals, because the operator does not publish regional actuals. The sector comparison uses the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero’s final 2024 territorial emissions.

Key definitions

  • PUE (power usage effectiveness): A facility’s total energy divided by its IT energy. Lower is better – 1.2 is efficient, 1.6 is not.
  • Scope 2 emissions: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, the operational carbon discussed here.
  • Scope 3 emissions: Other indirect emissions, including the embodied carbon in bought equipment and construction.
  • Embodied carbon: Emissions from making the building and equipment, before operation.
  • Average versus marginal intensity: The average grid is how the mix looks today; the marginal is what gets dispatched when new demand connects, which in Britain is usually gas.
  • REGO/PPA: Renewable energy guarantees of origin and power purchase agreements, the certificates and contracts behind “100% renewable” claims, which do not change the physical grid.
summary:
The UK’s existing stock of datacentres is smaller than suggested by most of the numbers in circulation, and so is the carbon it emits today. A fresh count by Computer Weekly puts the running estate at about 1.5GW (gigawatts) across roughly 90 to 110 sites, most of them clustered in London and the M4 corridor.

On today’s electricity grid, that estate emits about 1.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) a year. That is roughly the annual footprint of UK domestic aviation, or a third of the country’s cement sector.

But the committed pipeline of datacentres in the UK planning system – projects that have entered planning but are not yet built – stands at 173 projects and more than 14.6GW of capacity. That’s several times the size of the estate running today, as Computer Weekly has reported, and the carbon that pipeline would add is a different order of magnitude.

In this piece we estimate the carbon footprint of the UK’s datacentres three ways: what they emit in operation, what is locked into their construction and equipment, and how these compare with the rest of the UK economy.

title: AI minister talks up tech independence
raw_text:
During a speech given at Imperial College London’s science and tech incubator, Base One, artificial intelligence (AI) minister Kanishka Narayan emphasised the importance of Britain remaining technology agnostic. 

“We want the world’s leading companies to invest here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment,” he said.

Framing the government’s policy on AI around what matters to UK citizens, he said technology infrastructure should not be built simply because a company wants it. “We must be clear about what Britain needs and what our people receive in return,” said Narayan. “British national interest will be and must be our guiding principle.”

He warned that the country does not control the technology it uses. “Much of the technology that will shape our economy, our public services, and our national security is being developed outside this country,” said Narayan.

Discussing how the country has failed to build out on early successes in computing, such as semiconductor manufacturing, he said: “In 1978, James Callaghan’s government backed Inmos with £50m of public investment. Its pioneering work in Bristol and Newport helped establish an industrial legacy that remains important to South Wales’s semiconductor industry. Britain’s early leadership in personal computing helped give rise to Arm, now one of the world’s most important semiconductor design companies.”

However, Narayan admitted the country had given up this leadership. “The bitter lesson of the past is that an early lead in technology is not the same as retaining the power to shape its future,” he said.

The country’s reliance on technology that isn’t home-grown is, for Narayan, a question of national security, as well as what he called “a question of democratic power”. “If the British state cannot exercise meaningful control over the technologies on which our country depends, neither can the people that it represents,” he said.

Narayan wants working people to be able to influence how technology changes their jobs. “I will not accept a future in which Britain depends on technologies it cannot understand or control, while working people bear the costs of progress they have no power to shape,” he said. “Britain must have the power to build its own future and the British people must have the power to shape it.”

Narayan called on the developers of frontier to stop releasing unsafe AI systems. “I want cyber security discussed in every boardroom in Britain, rather than simply delegated to middle management,” he said. “And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviours. If you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system.”

In September, OpenAI admitted that one of its AI agents had accessed Australia’s Medicare Statistics portal in June. The UK government is now ramping up cyber security measures. Narayan said that alongside the Department for Culture, Media and Sport cyber minister and the security minister, he will be leading work on using frontier AI capabilities to find weaknesses in government systems before attackers exploit them.
